area.title: Story Creek
area.subtitle: Jesus stories that stick
area.blurb: The Teacher spoke in pictures — not to hide the truth, but to make it move.
area.intro: A creek path, oaks, and pictures you can hold: a road, a table, a lost coin in the dust.
Jesus taught in pictures. Play them. Then keep one true line.

lesson.title: The Good Samaritan
lesson.idea: neighbor is the one who shows mercy
lesson.claim: Neighbor is the one who shows mercy.
lesson.plain: A neighbor is the person who shows mercy — not the person who looks like you.

journal.title: The Teacher who taught in stories
journal.body: The Gospels present Jesus as a teacher whose most characteristic form is the parable. These are not children’s decorations added to a lecture. They are the lecture — they force a decision about mercy, pride, and the identity of God.

The Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37) relocates the word “neighbor” from a boundary question to a mercy question. The listener is not first invited to classify others. The listener is invited to become the kind of person who crosses the road.

easy.learn: Jesus tells a story. A hurt man lies on the road. Religious men walk past. A Samaritan is moved with compassion and helps. Then Jesus asks who *proved* to be a neighbor.

match.sentence: Neighbor is the one who shows mercy.

hold.why: First the hurt man, then help.
hold.claimMiss: Neighbor means the person who already looks like you.
The priest is the hero because he kept the law.
hold.whyMiss: The story is mainly a map of the Jericho road.
Mercy is optional once you have classified the victim.

medium.learn: Jesus makes the listener identify with the wounded man, then with the Samaritan moved with compassion.

hard.learn: Samaritans and Judeans were divided by worship and memory (see John 4:9). Jesus flips the question (Luke 10:36): mercy proves who the neighbor is. He makes the listener identify with the wounded man — and then with costly mercy.

lesson.title: The father’s run
lesson.idea: the father runs before the apology is finished
lesson.claim: The father runs with mercy before the speech is done.
lesson.plain: The father runs with mercy before the son finishes his speech.

journal.title: Mercy that runs
journal.body: Luke 15 stacks three lost-and-found stories after a complaint: this man welcomes sinners and eats with them. The father’s run (Luke 15:20) is the theological center of the third story. Honor is spent so that the son can be embraced before he finishes his hired-hand speech.
The older brother shows that you can live in the house and still refuse the feast. Nearness without joy at another’s return is a second lostness.

easy.learn: Jesus tells about a son who takes his share early and wastes it far from home. Hungry and ashamed, he starts a hired-hand speech to ask for work. But his father sees him while he is still a long way off and runs — mercy before the speech is done. He hugs the son. Honor is spent so the lost one can be welcomed; the feast is the father’s idea.

match.sentence: The father runs with mercy before the speech is done.

hold.claimMiss: The son earned the feast by writing a good apology.
The story is mainly about dividing an estate.
hold.whyMiss: The father waits until justice is complete.
The older brother is the hero for staying home.

medium.learn: Honor is spent so the son can be embraced; the older brother shows nearness without joy.

lesson.title: Pictures of the kingdom
lesson.idea: the kingdom arrives in pictures, not slogans
lesson.claim: The kingdom arrives in pictures, not slogans.
lesson.plain: The kingdom comes in Jesus stories you can hold — not slogans.

journal.title: Seeds, search, and a trust
journal.body: Taken together, the sower, the lost sheep, the mustard seed, and the talents sketch a God who speaks, seeks, grows a kingdom from small beginnings, and will ask what was done with a trust.
That is already a case of a sort: not a syllogism, but a coherent portrait. If the portrait is true, the world is personal before it is mechanical.

easy.learn: Soil, a search, a tiny seed, and a trust. Each Jesus story asks what you will do with what you heard.

match.sentence: The kingdom arrives in pictures, not slogans.

hold.why: Pictures tell it — not a slogan.
hold.claimMiss: Every parable is an allegory of every detail.
The kingdom is only for people who already understand.
hold.whyMiss: The sower proves every heart is the same.
The talents story is about hiding gifts until heaven.

medium.learn: Soil, search, a tiny seed, and a trust form a portrait — not a slogan.

lesson.title: An unpayable account
lesson.idea: received mercy makes refusing mercy a contradiction
lesson.claim: Received mercy makes refusing mercy a contradiction.
lesson.plain: If you were forgiven a huge debt, you cannot choke a neighbor over a small one.

journal.title: The measure you use
journal.body: Matthew 18:21–35 is severe because grace is severe in the opposite direction from cruelty: it creates a world. To be forgiven an unpayable debt and then throttle a neighbor is to live as if the king’s mercy never happened.
Jesus teaches his disciples to pray “forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” (Matt 6:12). The petition assumes the same moral grain.

easy.learn: A king wipes an unpayable bill. That same servant then chokes a neighbor over a tiny sum. Example: huge debt forgiven — then a tiny one demanded.

match.sentence: Received mercy makes refusing mercy a contradiction.

hold.why: He was forgiven much, then choked a neighbor.
hold.claimMiss: Forgiveness is a limited coupon on God’s spreadsheet.
Jesus is only reforming first-century banking.
hold.whyMiss: Peter’s “seven times” was already the full measure.
The first servant was right to demand prison.

medium.learn: The servant forgiven an unpayable debt then throttles a peer over a small sum.

match.sentence: Received mercy makes refusing mercy a contradiction.

hard.learn: Mercy is not softness. It is the grain of God’s world — and then a question: will you live against that grain? See also Matt 6:12–15.
